stimulus.title: The Clockmaker's Apprentice
stimulus.body: Inside Master Vance's narrow workshop on Collins Lane, sixty pendulums ticked in slightly different rhythms, creating a sound like steady rain on a timber roof. Twelve-year-old Elena spent her Saturdays sorting tiny brass gears onto velvet trays, learning to tell a worn pivot from a bent tooth by touch alone. One wet morning, a customer brought in a tarnished pocket watch that had stopped in 1924. 'Three repairers told me the mainspring is beyond saving,' the man sighed. Master Vance placed his loupe over one eye, studied the balance wheel for a full minute, and handed the watch to Elena. 'Don't look at what is broken,' he murmured. 'Find what is still true.' Elena gently brushed away decades of hardened oil with a pegwood stick. Beneath the grime, the escapement clicked once—faint, but unbroken—and a quiet grin spread across her face.

stimulus.title: Compasses in the Sky: How Migratory Birds Navigate
stimulus.body: Every autumn, bar-tailed godwits depart Alaska and fly non-stop across the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand and eastern Australia—a journey of over eleven thousand kilometres without landing once to eat or rest. How do birds weighing less than a loaf of bread cross featureless ocean with pinpoint accuracy? Decades of research suggest they rely not on a single trick, but on an overlapping suite of biological compasses. By day, birds track the sun's arc across the sky, adjusting for the time of day using an internal body clock. By night, many species orient themselves by the rotation of constellations around the celestial pole. Even under thick overcast skies, migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field through specialised light-sensitive proteins in their eyes and tiny iron-rich receptors in their beaks. Using multiple backup systems ensures that if cloud cover hides the stars or sun, the flock still stays on course.

workedSolution: The passage states 'a journey of over eleven thousand kilometres without landing once.'

stimulus.title: Compasses in the Sky: How Migratory Birds Navigate
stimulus.body: Every autumn, bar-tailed godwits depart Alaska and fly non-stop across the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand and eastern Australia—a journey of over eleven thousand kilometres without landing once to eat or rest. How do birds weighing less than a loaf of bread cross featureless ocean with pinpoint accuracy? Decades of research suggest they rely not on a single trick, but on an overlapping suite of biological compasses. By day, birds track the sun's arc across the sky, adjusting for the time of day using an internal body clock. By night, many species orient themselves by the rotation of constellations around the celestial pole. Even under thick overcast skies, migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field through specialised light-sensitive proteins in their eyes and tiny iron-rich receptors in their beaks. Using multiple backup systems ensures that if cloud cover hides the stars or sun, the flock still stays on course.
